summary:
RotaTerra
Agricultural Decision-Support System for Crop Rotation
RotaTerra is an agricultural decision-support system designed to help farmers in Cameroon
make better crop rotation decisions. It analyzes parcel-specific environmental and agro-
nomic information, including rainfall, temperature, soil moisture, slope, and crop require-
ments, using satellite data from NASA and agricultural references from FAO.
The system evaluates existing crop rotations according to seven criteria, such as drought
resilience, soil fertility, erosion protection, pest-cycle interruption, and climate suitability.
It also compares alternative rotations and provides transparent, evidence-based explana-
tions to support farmers’ decisions.
RotaTerra addresses the challenge of making agricultural decisions under changing cli-
matic and environmental conditions. It is important because it aims to promote more
sustainable farming practices, protect soil resources, reduce climate-related risks, and im-
prove long-term agricultural resilience. A planned blockchain component will also support
the traceability of agricultural products and raw materials.

RotaTerra — Project description

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

RotaTerra

A decision-support tool for crop rotation

built on NASA Earth observations

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Leveraging Earth Observation Data for Informed Agricultural

Decision-Making

Pilot area: Yaoundé and the Centre Region, Cameroon

In one sentence. RotaTerra lets a smallholder farmer draw their field on a map, enter

the rotation they currently practise, and instantly compare it with two alternative rotations,

criterion by criterion, with the evidence, the risks, the data gaps and a confidence level shown

for every result. The tool supports the farmer’s decision; it never makes it for them.

1 What exactly does it do?

Farmers around Yaoundé face irregular rains, dry spells, water erosion, acidic and nutrient-poor

soils, and pressure from pests and diseases. Choosing what to plant next, and in which order, is

hard: a crop that restores the soil in one place can fail on acid soils, find no buyer, or cost more

than the family can afford. RotaTerra turns long-term NASA observations and local agronomic

knowledge into practical, comparable information.

For a given field, RotaTerra does the following:

1. Locates and delimits the field. The farmer searches for a place, zooms on satellite imagery,

or uses the phone’s GPS, then draws the field boundary. The field can also be delimited remotely,

without being physically on it. The tool computes the area, slope and altitude.

2. Evaluates the current rotation. The farmer enters their rotation season by season (for

example maize in the first rainy season, groundnut in the second). RotaTerra gives it one score

per criterion.

3. Proposes two alternatives. A deterministic engine generates agronomically valid rotations

and keeps two contrasted ones: one oriented towards soil protection and one oriented towards

income.

4. Compares A, B and C side by side, showing the strengths, weaknesses and trade-offs of

each, the sources behind every score, the alerts and the confidence level.

5. Leaves the decision to the farmer, who chooses a rotation and may share it with the

community.

Seven criteria, and deliberately no single global score, so that no trade-off is hidden behind

an average:

CriterionWhat it tells the farmer

Drought resilience

Heat / frost stress

Erosion protection

Soil fertility

Pest-cycle breakHow often the crop would run short of water during its cycle

Exposure to temperatures beyond the crop’s limits

How long the soil stays bare, weighted by slope and extreme rainfall

Soil constraints (acidity, drainage, phosphorus) and nitrogen fixation

Whether botanical families alternate (for example no tomato followed by

pepper)

Sowing date versus the onset of the rains, and dry weather at harvest

Confirmed outlet for the crop and its use for the household

Calendar fit

Market / food security

Alerts are raised whatever the score when a critical situation is detected: no confirmed outlet,

household food security at risk, soil too constraining, cost above the declared budget, insecure land

tenure combined with late-yielding crops, or a legume on acidic, phosphorus-poor soil.

What RotaTerra does not do. It does not predict yields, does not recommend fertiliser or

pesticide doses, and does not replace the judgement of farmers or agronomists.

2.2 Data: offline preparation, fast online use

NASA and FAO data are downloaded and aggregated offline for the study area, then stored as a

pre-computed cache. At use time, the app reads only the cache, so responses are fast, work well

with limited connectivity, and are fully reproducible.

Datasets restricted to the United States (such as SSURGO or CropScape) were excluded because

they do not cover Cameroon. Soil data are the main gap: they rely on FAO GAEZ constraints and

the agronomic table, and are therefore displayed with a low confidence level until soil analyses are

available.

2.3 The scoring engine (rules, not a language model)

Scores are computed by explicit, reproducible rules: the same data always give the same notes.

Each criterion is calculated per season, then aggregated by keeping the worst case, since a rotation

is not resilient if one single season is exposed. Examples of the logic:

• Drought: a daily soil-water balance driven by crop evapotranspiration (ETc = Kc × ETo ,

FAO-56) gives the share of years in which the crop would be water-stressed.

• Erosion: months of bare soil, weighted by extreme rainfall and by slope, using a crop-cover

calendar.

2RotaTerra — Project description

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

• Pests: a penalty when the same crop or botanical family returns too soon, stronger for

high-pressure families such as Solanaceae.

Every note is expressed on a 0–100 scale and on five qualitative levels (very low to very high), and

carries a confidence level that depends on the number of years of data, the spatial resolution of the

source, and whether the agronomic parameters have been validated by an expert.

2.4 Alternative rotations

A deterministic engine generates candidate rotations under hard agronomic constraints (families

must alternate, cycles must fit the calendar, no excluded crop, outlet confirmed, within the declared

budget and land-tenure situation). It keeps the candidates that no other rotation beats on every

criterion at once (a Pareto selection) and picks two contrasted profiles, so that the farmer faces a

real choice.

2.5 Role of machine learning

Machine learning only measures climate risk; it never chooses a rotation. A supervised model

(random forest or gradient boosting) learns how vegetation (NDVI) responds to rainfall, temperature

and soil-moisture anomalies and produces a stress frequency per crop window; an unsupervised

model (k-means) groups weekly NDVI curves into typical seasons and bare-soil periods. A model is

kept only if it beats the climatological baseline on years held out; otherwise the system falls back

on the rules alone.

2.6 Grounded explanations

A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module turns the computed notes into plain-language

explanations. It retrieves passages from a curated knowledge base (local agronomic practice,

FAO-56, dataset documentation) and cites its sources. When no relevant passage exists, it says so

instead of inventing an answer, and a neutral fallback text is produced from the computed values

alone. The language model never modifies a score.

2.7 Traceability with blockchain (planned)

We plan to add a blockchain-based traceability layer for agricultural products and raw

materials.

• Each harvest batch receives a unique identifier linked to its crop, the rotation context and

the date.

• Key events (harvest, storage, transfer, processing, sale) are appended as tamper-evident

records.

• Buyers, cooperatives and consumers can verify the origin and history of a product or raw

material.

• Only hashes and minimal metadata are stored on-chain; precise field locations and personal

data stay off-chain, with the farmer’s consent.

The aim is to connect good rotation practices to verifiable proof of origin, and to help farmers

access markets that reward traceable, sustainable production.

3 What benefits does it have?

For farmers A simple path from drawing a field to comparing three rotations, with no technical

or geospatial background needed. It surfaces risks that are hard to see alone (bare-soil periods,

rainfall onset, pest cycles) and keeps the farmer’s own constraints at the centre: budget, outlet,

household food, land tenure, access to water.

Transparency and trust Every score points to a rule or a cited data source, shows its confidence

level and its data gaps, so users know when a result rests on a fragile basis.

For agronomists and extension services A single place to review the rules and the crop table,

comment on a farmer’s rotation and contribute field observations (IRAD, ITA, MINADER and

others).

For land and soil Encourages rotations that shorten bare-soil periods, limit erosion, break pest

cycles and use nitrogen-fixing crops wisely.

For markets Traceable products and raw materials can strengthen buyers’ trust and open access

to demanding markets.

Low cost and reproducible Built on free, open NASA and FAO data and open-source tools,

with pre-computed data that keep running costs low.

4 What do you hope to achieve?

• During the hackathon: deliver a working core: field delimitation, evaluation of the current

rotation, two alternatives, and a clear comparison with evidence, alerts and confidence.

• Pilot in Yaoundé: validate the rules and the crop table with agronomists (IRAD Nkolbisson,

ITA, MINADER) and with partner farmers, and calibrate the parameters on local data and soil

analyses.

• Improve over time: refine the machine-learning indicators as data series grow, enrich the

knowledge base with expert contributions, and develop the community space where farmers

share parcels and rotations.

• Extend: adapt the crop table and the rules to other agro-ecological zones of Cameroon and,

later, to other countries, without redesigning the system.

• Connect practices to markets: link rotation decisions to blockchain-based traceability so

that sustainable practices become verifiable.

• Keep the right role for technology: remain a support tool that informs the farmer, never a

substitute for their judgement or for local expertise.

4RotaTerra — Project description

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Hardware. No specialised hardware is required. We developed and tested on standard laptops,

and the web app is designed to be used on smartphones, tablets and computers, including the

phone’s GPS for field mapping. Heavy data processing runs offline on a laptop or a server, and the

application only reads the pre-computed results.

Use of artificial intelligence. Machine-learning models are used only to estimate climate-risk

indicators. A language model is used only to write grounded explanations from retrieved sources.

Generative AI assistants also supported us in design discussions, documentation and code drafting;

the team reviewed and tested all outputs. No scoring decision is delegated to a language model.

Responsible use. Results are decision support, not predictions. Satellite pixels (for example

about 9 km for SMAP and 250 m for MODIS) can be larger than a smallholder’s field, so

indicators are aggregated and shown with a confidence level. Agronomic rules and parameters

must be reviewed by local experts before wide use.
